analysis.one_liner: Raises the salary level under which salaried workers must receive overtime pay, with automatic annual updates.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the House Education and the Workforce Committee in March 2023, never received a hearing, markup, or vote, and died when the 118th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Under federal law, salaried executive, administrative, and professional workers who earn above a set salary can be denied overtime pay. This bill would raise that cutoff from about $35,568 to $45,000 immediately, then step it up to $55,000, $65,000, and $75,000 over three years, and tie it to the 55th percentile of full-time salaried earnings after 2027 so it rises automatically. It would also tighten the rules so an employee who spends 20% or more of the time on non-management work could not be classified as exempt, and it would require the government to publish the wage data used to set the threshold.
analysis.who_benefits: Millions of salaried workers earning between the current threshold and the new one — supervisors, office managers, and white-collar staff in retail, restaurants, banking, and insurance — who would become entitled to time-and-a-half pay for hours over 40 per week. Workers who keep their salaried-exempt status would also gain from the tighter duties test.

how_it_helps.text: Raises the overtime eligibility cutoff to $45,000 on the effective date, then $55,000 in 2024, $65,000 in 2025, and $75,000 in 2026, up from the roughly $35,568 level in effect since 2019.

Beginning in 2027, ties the threshold to the 55th percentile of weekly earnings for full-time salaried workers nationally — projected in the bill's findings at about $82,745 by 2026 — and updates it automatically every year without a new rulemaking, so it keeps pace with wages rather than stagnating for decades.

Bars the overtime exemption for any salaried employee who spends at least 20% of their time on duties unrelated to executive or administrative work, targeting businesses that give workers minor management titles while paying them for ordinary labor.
Directs the Bureau of Labor Statistics to publish quarterly data on weekly earnings of full-time salaried workers by region, making the data behind the threshold public.

analysis.who_pays: Employers of salaried staff in the affected pay band — retail chains, restaurants, hotels, banks, insurers, and other businesses that rely on long hours from low-paid salaried managers and administrators — through overtime premiums, wage adjustments, or limits on scheduled hours.
analysis.who_pays_short: Employers of salaried staff in that band

drawbacks.text: The phase-up to the 55th percentile of earnings (projected at about $82,745 by 2026) is a steep increase, and employers in lower-wage regions would face the same national cutoff despite local pay levels.

Businesses could respond by reclassifying salaried staff as hourly, converting salaried pay to lower base wages plus overtime, or capping hours, so some workers could end up with the same or lower take-home pay and less schedule flexibility.

Tightening the duties test to a 20% limit would remove exempt status from many working supervisors — such as restaurant and retail managers who mix hands-on work with management — raising labor costs that could be passed on to consumers through prices.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit is real and targeted: overtime eligibility for a large group of salaried workers who now work extra hours for free. The costs fall on employers in affected pay bands and could reach consumers through prices or reach workers through reduced hours and base pay. The steepest design risk is the automatic annual escalation to a national wage percentile with no regional adjustment, which makes the long-run level less responsive to economic conditions than the phased step-ups. On balance the bill would shift income from employers to a well-defined group of salaried workers, and the honest case against it is about timing, regional fit, and possible employer workarounds rather than the underlying goal.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the House Education and the Workforce Committee from the day it was introduced until the Congress ended, with no hearing, no markup, and no floor vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Mark Takano introduced the bill on March 29, 2023, joined by Rep. Alma Adams, and it was referred to the House Committee on Education and the Workforce the same day.
29 House members cosponsored the bill, all Democrats.

The bill's only actions were its introduction and committee referral; no subcommittee or full committee action, hearing, or vote appears in its history before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.
The bill's findings argue the overtime threshold had eroded: in 1975 about 63% of full-time salaried workers were guaranteed overtime, but by 2022 less than 15% were.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Businesses that rely on long hours from salaried employees earning between about $35,568 and $82,745 kept paying no overtime for that work. The bill's supporters gained nothing from its death.

for.name: Rep. Mark Takano
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Restoring Overtime Pay Act and guided its introduction phase.

for.name: Rep. Alma Adams
for.what_they_did: Joined Takano at introduction as the bill's co-lead in the House.

for.name: 29 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors; the bill drew no Republican cosponsors.

against.name: House Committee on Education and the Workforce
against.role: Committee of referral in the 118th Congress
against.what_they_did: Held the bill without a hearing, markup, or vote from referral in March 2023 until the Congress ended.

against.name: Rep. Virginia Foxx
against.role: Chair, House Education and the Workforce Committee
against.what_they_did: As committee chair, controlled the markup calendar and never scheduled the bill for consideration.

against.name: House Republican leadership
against.what_they_did: Controlled the floor calendar and never brought the bill up; with a Republican majority and no Republican cosponsors, it had no path to a floor vote.

sides.party_line_note: All 29 cosponsors were Democrats and the bill was referred to a committee chaired by a Republican; no Republican signed on, and the bill never advanced in the Republican-controlled House.

industries.note: These industries rely heavily on salaried store, restaurant, and shift managers in the $35,000–$82,000 band who work long hours without overtime. The bill would require overtime pay or tighter scheduling for them, a direct labor-cost increase.
Many low-paid administrative and paraprofessional salaried staff in these sectors fall just above the current threshold. The bill would raise their cost of long working weeks.

industries.industry: Staffing, payroll, and HR compliance services
industries.note: Reclassifying large numbers of salaried employees and administering a rising, annually updated threshold would create compliance work for these firms.
